summary:
Kuwait's Penal Code Article 198 was amended in 2007 by Article 199 bis, which criminalised an indecent act in a public place or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars, about US$3,500. The amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support. Human Rights Watch found that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor obtain protection from the policing it authorised.

In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck down the provision as unconstitutional, after an individual who had been targeted by police challenged it. The ruling removed the criminal exposure the article created; it did not end the dress-code policing that preceded and outlasted it. Human Rights Watch called on parliament to repeal the law outright rather than leave the matter to the court's decision.

Enforcement of the 2007 provision was immediate. Within two weeks of it taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, in coffee shops and in taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as a punishment. Appearance-based policing continued after the article's annulment: in 2017 a social media figure was arrested in Kuwait for allegedly looking too feminine and held for two weeks before release.

Penal Code Article 193 continues to punish consensual same-sex relations between men by up to seven years in prison, and adultery by up to five. Public morality laws are strictly enforced and prosecutions of LGBTQ people are routine. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship, or whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status, falls within the reach of that provision.

A year after the Constitutional Court ruling, DAWN MENA reported that discrimination against transgender people continued in practice and that the decision had not opened a path to recognising transgender rights. The ruling is a limit on state power, not a change in the wider legal regime.

Kuwait's communications regulator, CITRA, has blocked LGBTQI+ material online, including advocacy and legal information. Censors banned the film 'The Danish Girl', and in August 2023 banned 'Barbie' on the claim that it promoted homosexuality; in July 2019 the Ministry of Commerce carried out a crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops.

On entry screening, it was announced in September 2013 that all Gulf Cooperation Council states had agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of testing to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners. Officials later insisted it was only a proposal, and concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar was cited as a reason for backtracking. No source documents the proposal being implemented.

Foreigners found to be infected with HIV/AIDS are deported, while Kuwaiti citizens who are infected are entitled to outpatient care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence has remained under 0.1 percent through the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25 to 49 making up 47 percent of those with HIV. In 1992 the National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV.
tangentialFactors:
Cross-dressing is criminalised across much of the region, and gender segregation combined with enforced dress codes leaves trans people especially vulnerable; a 2016 regional survey records this pattern and notes that censors in Kuwait banned 'The Danish Girl' alongside other jurisdictions.

Human Rights Watch's 2018 study of LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa covered 22 jurisdictions and drew on interviews with 34 activists. Six interviewees, from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco, had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or their activism.

The 2022 annulment came from an individual challenge by someone the police had targeted, not from a legislative initiative. Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute's July 2024 analysis set out the steps still required after abolition, and the 2007 amendment's passage with overwhelming parliamentary support stands in contrast to the court's later decision.
localsOnly:
No association or charity is known to exist in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or to organise educational and social events for the community. A group of Kuwaitis applied in 2007 to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form such an association and never received a formal reply; in July 2019 they announced they would reapply.

Transgender residents face social and employment discrimination that the 2022 Constitutional Court ruling did not address.

In the 2023 National Assembly elections no candidate ran while openly acknowledging an LGBTQI+ orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council testing proposal was ever implemented is unresolved. Officials described it as a proposal only and cited the 2022 World Cup as a reason for backtracking; no source documents testing at Kuwaiti ports of entry.

Parliament had not repealed Article 198 as of the sources. Human Rights Watch's call for outright repeal and Cairo 52's analysis of post-abolition steps leave the legislative position unresolved.

The scale of dress-code policing after February 2022 is not quantified. DAWN MENA documents continuing discrimination but no systematic enforcement data.

Sources describe the struck provision both as Article 198 and as the 2007 amendment Article 199 bis; the two references are not reconciled in the available material.

No youth-specific or minor-specific HIV care access provisions are documented, and whether the 2019 reapplication for an LGBTQ association received a response is not sourced.
